questions.question: A hundredths grid is one whole square cut into 100 equal small squares. Ava shades 37 whole small squares and half of one more small square, so 37.5 small squares are shaded. Which decimal and percent name the shaded part?
questions.explain: Each small square is one hundredth, so 37.5 shaded squares means 37.5 hundredths = 37.5 ÷ 100 = 0.375, and 'per hundred' makes it 37.5%. The trap is sliding the decimal point the wrong way and writing 3.75, which would be more than the whole grid.

questions.question: On a hundredths grid of 100 equal small squares (the whole grid is 1), Leo shades 6 whole small squares and half of one more, so 6.5 small squares are shaded. Written as a decimal, how much of the grid is shaded?
questions.explain: 6.5 shaded squares out of 100 is 6.5 hundredths, and 6.5 ÷ 100 = 0.065 (which is also 6.5%). A common slip is moving the decimal point only one place and writing 0.65 — that would be 65 shaded squares, ten times too many.

questions.question: A hundredths grid has 100 equal small squares and stands for one whole. Priya shades 12 whole small squares plus half of one more, so 12.5 small squares are shaded. What percent of the grid is shaded?
questions.explain: Percent means 'out of 100', so 12.5 shaded squares out of 100 squares is exactly 12.5% (and 0.125 as a decimal). Watch out: 125% would be more than one whole grid, which is impossible when only part of one grid is shaded.

questions.question: A hundredths grid is one whole and is cut into 100 equal small squares. Kai wants to shade 0.062 of the whole grid. How many small squares should Kai shade, and what percent is that?
options: 0.62 of one small square, which is 0.62%
questions.explain: Going from a decimal to hundredths, 0.062 × 100 = 6.2, so 6.2 of the 100 small squares get shaded and that is 6.2%. The trap is dropping the thousandths digit and shading 62 squares, which would be 0.62 — ten times too much.

questions.question: Which percent is equal to the fraction 5/8?
questions.explain: Divide the numerator by the denominator: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625, then multiply by 100 (decimal point two places right) to get 62.5%. The usual mistake is keeping the same digits as the decimal and writing 0.625%, which is a tiny amount, not more than half.

questions.question: A hardware store in Kamloops says that 0.4% of its light bulbs arrive broken. Written as a decimal, what is 0.4%?
questions.explain: To turn a percent into a decimal, divide by 100, so 0.4 ÷ 100 = 0.004 (the decimal point moves two places left, not one). Writing 0.4 keeps the percent as a plain number, which would mean 40% of the bulbs were broken.

questions.question: Ravi's water bottle holds 750 mL when full, and right now it is 7/8 full. Which decimal and percent describe how full the bottle is?
questions.explain: Divide first: 7 ÷ 8 = 0.875, then move the decimal point two places right for the percent, 87.5%. A decimal for part of a whole must be less than 1, so 8.75 signals the decimal point was shifted the wrong way.

questions.question: Mia converts the fraction 2/3 and gets a repeating decimal. Which pair correctly gives the repeating decimal and the percent, with the percent rounded to one decimal place?
questions.explain: 2 ÷ 3 = 0.666… (a repeating decimal), and multiplying by 100 moves the decimal point two places right to give 66.66…%, which rounds to 66.7%. Rounding before converting, or keeping the decimal's digits as the percent, gives answers far too small for a fraction close to 1.

questions.question: In Ms. Lam's class, 9 of the 24 students bike to school. In Mr. Singh's class, 36% of the students bike to school. Which class has the greater percent of bikers, and by how much?
questions.explain: Convert the fraction first: 9 ÷ 24 = 0.375, then × 100 gives 37.5%, and 37.5% − 36% = 1.5%. The common trap is treating 0.375 as 0.375% (or shifting only one place to get 3.75%), which makes Ms. Lam's class look far smaller than it really is.

questions.question: Jonah says, 'The decimal 0.5 is the same as 5%, because you just move the decimal point one place.' Which statement about Jonah's thinking is correct?
options: Jonah is right: moving the decimal point one place to the right turns 0.5 into 5%.
Jonah is wrong: 0.5 = 50%, because 0.5 means 50 hundredths, and 5% would be the decimal 0.05.
Jonah is wrong: 0.5 = 500%, because you move the decimal point three places to the right.
Jonah is wrong: 0.5 = 0.5%, because the percent uses the same number as the decimal.
questions.explain: Percent means hundredths, so a decimal becomes a percent by multiplying by 100 — two places right: 0.5 → 50%. Check by going backwards: 5% ÷ 100 = 0.05, not 0.5, so one place is always one place too few.

questions.question: At a school bake sale in Surrey, 3 of every 8 muffins sold were banana muffins. A poster says 'Over 40% of our muffins were banana!' Which statement about the poster is correct?
options: No — 3/8 = 0.375, so only 0.375% of the muffins were banana.
questions.explain: Convert the fraction to compare: 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375, and × 100 gives 37.5%, just under 40%, so the poster is wrong. The frequent error is keeping 0.375 as 0.375% or shifting one place to 3.75% — both would say almost no muffins were banana, but 3 out of 8 is close to half.

questions.question: Nick's soccer team won 13 of its 20 games this season. Ana's team won 0.7 of its games. Whose team won the greater percent of its games?
questions.explain: Put both in the same form: 13 ÷ 20 = 0.65 = 65%, and 0.7 = 0.70 = 70%, so Ana's team is higher. The trap is reading 0.7 as 7% (one shift instead of two) or as 0.7%, which wrongly makes Ana's team look like the weaker one.
